theory.intro: Every angle standing on the same arc is fixed in size by that arc. The angle at the centre and the angle at the circumference are linked by a fixed ratio, and the angle in a semicircle is the special case.
steps: Identify the arc that the angle(s) stand on.
Decide the relationship: angle at centre and angle at circumference (double or halve), or two angles at the circumference on the same arc (equal).
Check whether the central angle needed is the reflex angle (vertex of the circumference angle on the minor arc).
Write the equation from the property and solve for the unknown.

foundation.solution_text:
$\angle ACB = \angle AOB \div 2$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc)
$x = 130^{\circ} \div 2$
$= 65^{\circ}$

$\angle AOB = \angle ACB \times 2$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc)
$x = 37^{\circ} \times 2$
$= 74^{\circ}$

The angle in a semicircle is $90^{\circ}$.
$x = 90^{\circ}$

$\angle ADB = \angle ACB$ (angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal)
$x = 48^{\circ}$

$\angle ADB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle AEB = \angle ACB$ (angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal)
$x = 52^{\circ}$
$y = 52^{\circ}$

$\angle ACB = 90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle)
$\angle ABC = 180^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} - 34^{\circ}$ (angle sum of $\triangle ABC$)
$x = 56^{\circ}$

$\angle ACB = \angle AOB \div 2$ and $\angle ADB = \angle AOB \div 2$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference)
$x = 96^{\circ} \div 2 = 48^{\circ}$
$y = 96^{\circ} \div 2 = 48^{\circ}$

development.solution_text:
$C$ is on the minor arc, so $\angle ACB$ stands on the major arc, and the matching central angle is the reflex $\angle AOB$.
Reflex $\angle AOB = \angle ACB \times 2$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc)
$x = 125^{\circ} \times 2$
$= 250^{\circ}$

$C$ is on the major arc, so the minor central angle $\angle AOB = 40^{\circ} \times 2 = 80^{\circ}$.
$D$ is on the minor arc, so $\angle ADB$ stands on the major arc, matching the reflex central angle $= 360^{\circ} - 80^{\circ} = 280^{\circ}$.
$x = 280^{\circ} \div 2$
$= 140^{\circ}$

$\angle ACB = 90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle), so $\triangle ABC$ is right-angled at $C$.
$BC = \sqrt{AB^2 - AC^2}$
$= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2}$
$= \sqrt{169 - 25}$
$= \sqrt{144}$
$= 12$ cm

$\angle AOB = \angle ACB \times 2 = 80^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference)
$OA = OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles.
$\angle OAB = (180^{\circ} - 80^{\circ}) \div 2$ (angle sum of $\triangle OAB$, base angles equal)
$x = 50^{\circ}$

Zara is not correct.
Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, regardless of exactly where the vertex sits on that arc.
So $\angle ACB = \angle ADB$, even though $C$ and $D$ are different points.

$C$ is on the minor arc, so $\angle ACB$ stands on the major arc, matching the reflex central angle.
$\angle ACB = \text{reflex } \angle AOB \div 2$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc)
$x = 220^{\circ} \div 2$
$= 110^{\circ}$

mastery.solution_text:
$OA = OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OAC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OAC = \angle OCA$.
$\angle AOD = \angle OAC + \angle OCA$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OAC$)
$= 2\angle OCA$
$OB = OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OBC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OBC = \angle OCB$.
$\angle BOD = \angle OBC + \angle OCB$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OBC$)
$= 2\angle OCB$
$\angle AOB = \angle AOD + \angle BOD$ ($D$ lies inside $\angle AOB$)
$= 2\angle OCA + 2\angle OCB$
$= 2(\angle OCA + \angle OCB)$
$= 2\angle ACB$

$\angle AOB = \angle ACB \times 2 = 70^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference)
$OA = OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles, with $\angle OAB = \angle OBA$.
$\angle OAB = (180^{\circ} - 70^{\circ}) \div 2$ (angle sum of $\triangle OAB$)
$= 55^{\circ}$
$\angle OBA = \angle OAB = 55^{\circ}$ (base angles of the isosceles triangle)

$E$ lies on the same arc as $C$ and $D$, so $\angle AEB$ also stands on the same arc as $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$.
Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, no matter how many points lie on that arc.
$\angle AEB = 42^{\circ}$
